title: Claude's new AI report card can flag AI 'inefficiencies' to employers

content_html:
Claude's new AI report card tool gives companies a closer look at costs — and flags 'inefficiencies'

By Natalie Musumeci

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

Anthropic is giving corporate customers a new way to scrutinize how their employees use its artificial intelligence chatbot Claude — and how much the AI work is costing them.

The AI giant announced "smart reports" for Claude Enterprise users last week. The interactive chart tool is designed to analyze a sample of a team's AI session transcripts and group work into categories, including the types of tasks employees use Claude for, the outputs it generates, and the cost.

The reports can also — and this is the part that is undoubtedly making teams sit up straight — flag "inefficiencies" to employers, including sessions that produced "no work value" or were "personal or off-topic," according to a Claude support webpage.

In effect, the smart reports tool offers companies equipped with Claude Enterprise something of an AI report card. Each organization can run up to 10 reports a month at no charge.

One caveat that Anthropic highlighted as "important" in its support documentation: "Smart reports help you understand adoption and plan your investment in Claude. They aren't designed and should not be used for evaluating individual performance or making employment decisions."

To produce a report, bosses can select a team, a time range of up to the last 28 days, the Claude products to include, focus areas for analysis, and any custom questions they want Claude to answer while analyzing the transcripts.

"Claude then reads a sample of transcripts in that scope, groups them into workstreams and types of outputs, attaches spend to each group, and writes up what it found," the Claude support page says.

According to Anthropic, sessions involving "restricted topics" — including personal conversations related to race, ethnicity, health, legal issues, union activity, and political or religious views — are "used only for aggregate analysis and don't include summaries."

"Personal conversations also don't include individual sessions or names," the Claude support page says.

An Anthropic spokesperson told Business Insider on Monday that smart reports do not show employees' names by default, but those settings can be changed.

"A report groups a team's work with Claude into workstreams and shows what each one cost. Opening a workstream shows short session summaries, not transcripts," the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson added, "An organization's owner can turn on a setting that allows names to be shown with those summaries. When that setting is turned on, names remain hidden until someone viewing the report chooses to reveal them, and each reveal is logged."

Sessions Claude identifies as personal or off-topic won't appear with names, the spokesperson said.

The launch of smart reports comes as many companies are trying to get a handle on AI costs and measure any productivity gains. Some are wrestling with how broadly to let employees use AI tools.

Bloomberg reported Monday that Goldman Sachs recently limited access to Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub coding tools to engineers only after assessing productivity and risk concerns. The move reportedly rankled some Goldman traders who used the tools for their work.

Her coverage often focused on stories at the intersection of law, business, politics, and technology. Natalie has covered Donald Trump’s criminal and civil cases, the wave of lawsuits against the second Trump administration, the indictment and criminal trial of Sean “Diddy” Combs, the shooting death of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, and the legal battles facing Elon Musk and his companies. Natalie came to Business Insider in June 2021 as a breaking news reporter, focusing on the most interesting angles on the day's trending news. Natalie largely drove BI’s coverage around the fatal “Rust” shooting involving Alec Baldwin and the disappearance and murder of Gabby Petito.Prior to joining BI, Natalie worked for the New York Post, the New York Daily News, and The Brooklyn Paper. She has an extensive background covering crime and courts. During her more than 12-year journalism career, she did a stint covering the police beat out of the New York Police Department's headquarters. Natalie, a Brooklyn native, graduated from Brooklyn College in 2012 with a degree in journalism.
